title: Splitwise split strategies
idea: A split strategy turns one expense total into per-user shares; each rule (equal, percent, exact) is its own class behind one `SplitStrategy` interface.
points: This is the Strategy pattern from c08: one method, `split(totalCents)`, many rules.
Each rule needs different inputs, so each strategy takes them in its constructor.
Integer division drops cents; hand leftover cents out in a fixed, documented order.
A new rule, such as split by units, is one new class.

steps.caption: The caller picks a strategy and configures it with its own inputs: 33.33%, 33.33% and 33.34%.
Percents arrive as integer basis points (1% = 100), so 33.33% is 3333. They must total 10000, checked up front.
Each share rounds down: 33.33% of 1000 cents is 333.3, which becomes 333.
One cent is left. It goes to the first user, Asha, even though Chen's percent is largest: simple and deterministic.
The `Expense` re-checks that shares equal the total. A correct strategy always passes.
An `ExactSplit` whose amounts total 900 throws inside `split(1000)`. No `Expense` is ever created.

code.title: The problem: one switch
code.caption: Every rule in one `switch`: cents leak, exact amounts go unchecked, and new rules edit old code.

walk.text: An enum of types is the usual start. Each value hides a different algorithm.
One signature for all rules, so `inputs` means something different per type.
Integer division rounds down, and the lost cents are never handed out.
Percent leaks cents the same way.
Exact amounts are trusted blindly, even when they miss the total.
A fourth rule means editing this method again. That breaks OCP.
The printout shows each sum next to the real total.

code.title: The fix: strategies
code.caption: One interface, a weighted strategy for equal and percent, and an exact strategy that validates. Users are plain names here to keep the file short.

walk.text: One method and one contract: the shares always sum to the total, or the call throws.
Equal and percent are both weights. Static factories check each rule's own inputs.
The private constructor guards shared rules and copies inputs, so callers cannot change them later.
Each share rounds down first. Multiplying before dividing keeps the precision.
Fewer than n cents remain. The first users get one each: deterministic, nothing lost.
Exact needs no rounding, only a check that the amounts match the total.
The caller depends only on `SplitStrategy`. It never asks which rule it holds.

pitfalls: Stopping at integer division loses cents; assert that shares sum to the total.
Taking percents as `double` invites rounding bugs; accept integer basis points instead.
A `switch` on `SplitType` inside the service grows with every rule and breaks OCP.

quiz.q: Same classes as the fix. Which cents does this print, in order?
quiz.why: Each share rounds down to 250, leaving 2 cents. The leftover loop gives one cent each to the first two users.

takeaway: One interface, one class per rule, and every cent assigned.

starters: Who should choose the SplitStrategy: the UI, a factory or the service?
Is giving leftover cents to the first users fair, and what are alternatives?
How would I add a split by shares, like 2 units for Asha and 1 for Ben?
